subtype: Stamping and slamming out in anger [Regulating]
passage: I'm Eshaan. At carrom time, Chinmay lost an argument about whether the striker had touched the line. He stamped his foot twice, said “Fine!” and walked out of the room. I expected him to sulk all break. Instead he walked to the end of the corridor and back, twice, with his fists clenched and then loose. Our class rule is that you may take a walk and come back to talk. When he returned, he sat down and said, “I still think it was a foul, but I shouldn't have stormed out.” I couldn't tell how angry he still was.

qa.q: What did Chinmay do twice before walking out?
qa.a: He stamped his foot twice.

qa.q: What might Chinmay have been feeling when he stamped and said “Fine!”, and what else could it be?
qa.a: Probably anger and frustration at losing the argument. He may also have needed to leave before he said something worse, and Eshaan admits not being able to tell how angry Chinmay still was.

qa.q: How did the walk-and-return rule turn the impulse into something safe?
qa.a: It let Chinmay leave and cool down without slamming or shouting, and then return to talk, so the feeling became a boundary and not a fight.

qa.q: How might Eshaan feel watching Chinmay walk out?
qa.a: Probably worried or awkward at first, then relieved when Chinmay came back to talk. Eshaan seems to respect the rule.

grounding: A child stamps out after losing an argument and uses a cooling-off walk before returning to talk.

subtype: Stamping and slamming out in anger [Regulating]
passage:
Monday: Jahnavi lost the argument about who got the tablet first. She stamped to her room and slammed the door. Her brother Rafiq shouted, “Don't be so dramatic!” and neither spoke at dinner.
Wednesday: Amma sat with Jahnavi and said, “When you're very angry, you can walk round the courtyard, and then come back and tell us what you think.”
Friday: Jahnavi lost another argument with Rafiq. She stamped once, said, “I'm going for my walk,” and left. Ten minutes later she came back. “I still want a turn,” she said. “Okay,” said Rafiq. “Sorry I shouted.”

qa.q: What did Amma suggest Jahnavi could do when she was very angry?
qa.a: She suggested she could walk round the courtyard and then come back and tell them what she thinks.

qa.q: What was Jahnavi probably feeling when she stamped and slammed the door on Monday, and what else could it be?
qa.a: Anger at losing the argument, and probably a need to get away. She may also have felt hurt at being called dramatic.

qa.q: What changed between Monday and Friday?
qa.a: Jahnavi used the cooling-off routine: she said she was going for a walk, left, and came back to talk, so the anger did not turn into slamming.

qa.q: How might Rafiq feel on Friday when Jahnavi comes back?
qa.a: Probably relieved that the fight did not blow up, and a little sorry, since he apologised for shouting.

grounding: A child stamps and slams the door in anger; a cooling-off walk and return makes a safe boundary.

subtype: Stamping and slamming out in anger [Regulating]
passage: Karthik, you slammed that door so hard the calendar fell. Let your Farida Nani tell you something. When I was ten, my brother Yunus and I fought over whose turn it was with the radio. He won, because he was older and louder. I stamped across the courtyard so hard my anklets rang, and I slammed the kitchen door. My Abba didn't shout. That evening he said, “Next time, stamp all the way to the mango tree. Touch it. Walk back slowly. Then talk.” At the next fight, I did it. By the time I came back, the fire in my chest had gone down, and I could say, “It's not fair, you always choose.” Yunus actually listened.

qa.q: What did Farida and Yunus fight over?
qa.a: They fought over whose turn it was with the radio.

qa.q: What was young Farida feeling when she stamped across the courtyard?
qa.a: She felt angry and powerless after losing to her older, louder brother, and needed to get away.

qa.q: What choice did Farida make in the next fight, and why did it help?
qa.a: She walked to the mango tree and back before talking, which let her anger cool so she could say calmly what felt unfair.

qa.q: How might Yunus have experienced the calmer Farida?
qa.a: Yunus probably found it easier to listen to a calm complaint than to a slammed door.

grounding: Shows a child stamping and slamming out after losing an argument, and a walk-then-talk routine turning the impulse into a safe boundary.

subtype: Stamping and slamming out in anger [Regulating]
passage: The rain had kept everyone inside the one-room flat for three days. When Gautam won the argument over the TV remote again, Ganga jumped up, stamped her foot so hard the steel glasses rattled, and headed for the door. Then she stopped. Outside was a wall of rain. There was nowhere to storm off to. Her fists shook. Maa pointed at the little balcony corner behind the curtain. “Your cooling spot. Ten slow breaths, then come back and say it.” Ganga pulled the curtain shut and watched the rain drip off the rail. Breath by breath, her shoulders dropped. She came back in. “Gautam, can we take turns every half hour?”

qa.q: How long had the rain kept everyone inside?
qa.a: The rain had kept everyone inside for three days.

qa.q: What was Ganga feeling when her fists shook at the door?
qa.a: She felt angry and trapped, with nowhere to storm off to in the rain.

qa.q: Why did the cooling spot work even in a small flat?
qa.a: It gave Ganga a place to step away and breathe, then return to talk, so her anger became a clear request.

qa.q: What would the evening be like for Gautam if Ganga had kept stamping?
qa.a: Gautam would probably have felt annoyed or defensive, and the fight over the remote would have gone on.

grounding: Shows a child stamping in anger after losing an argument, and a cooling-off routine letting her step away and return to talk.

subtype: Stamping and slamming out in anger [Regulating]
passage: In their flat in Ahmedabad, Jagdish lost the argument about the sleepover. “No, and that's final,” his father, Mohit, said. Jagdish stamped down the hallway, and the bedroom door slammed so hard the photo frames shook. He threw himself on the bed, heart hammering. Then he remembered the deal they'd made last month: storm out if you must, but come back within fifteen minutes and talk. He got up, went down the stairs, walked three laps round the building's car park and climbed back up. His father was waiting at the table. “I'm still angry,” Jagdish said. “But why no?” “Sit,” said Mohit. “I'll tell you properly.”

qa.q: How many laps did Jagdish walk round the car park?
qa.a: Jagdish walked three laps round the building's car park.

qa.q: What was Jagdish feeling as he threw himself on the bed?
qa.a: He felt furious and hurt at losing the argument, his heart hammering.

qa.q: How did the deal help Jagdish and his father?
qa.a: It let Jagdish leave to cool off but come back within fifteen minutes to talk, turning a slammed door into a real conversation.

qa.q: What might Mohit have felt while waiting at the table?
qa.a: Mohit may have felt worried but hopeful that Jagdish would keep the deal, and ready to explain properly.

grounding: Shows a child storming off and slamming a door after losing an argument, and an agreed walk-then-return routine.

subtype: Stamping and slamming out in anger [Regulating]
passage:
"No cricket until the project's done, Mridul. That's final."
"But everyone's going! You never—"
"I heard you. The answer's still no," said his stepdad, Francis.
"This is SO unfair!" Stamp, stamp, stamp down the corridor. BANG went the bedroom door.

Later: knock, knock. "Can I come in?"
"…Fine."
"You were really angry. It's okay to need to leave. Slamming the door, not so okay."
"You didn't even listen."
"Then let's make a deal. Next time, say 'I need a walk,' go round the building, and when you come back we talk properly. I'll listen then. Deal?"
"…Can it be round the building twice?"
"Twice is fine."

qa.q: What was Mridul not allowed to go to until the project was done?
qa.a: Cricket.

qa.q: What was Mridul feeling as he stamped down the corridor?
qa.a: Furious and unheard, sure the rule was unfair, and needing to get away from the argument.

qa.q: What cooling-off routine did they agree on?
qa.a: Mridul says "I need a walk", goes round the building (twice is fine), and then comes back to talk while Francis listens.

qa.q: How might Francis feel hearing the door bang?
qa.a: He is probably annoyed at the slam but can also see how angry Mridul is, which is why he comes to talk instead of shouting back.

grounding: It shows a child stamping off and slamming a door after losing an argument, and an adult turning the urge to leave into a walk-then-talk routine.
